## Case Studies

Sutherland SK, Tibballs J, (2001) Australian Animal Toxins, Oxford University Press.

No personal records of cases, but notes "bites by Suta suta are reported to be very painful for 30 minutes or so." Also notes Anthony (Anthony M (1998) Report of the bite of a Curl snake (Suta suta). Herpetofauna 28:11-13.) statesthat a bite by a 35cm specimen caused local stinging and swelling, followed by urticaria and pharyngeal oedema, which he opines is consistent with an allergic reaction; the patient had been bitten previously.

## Clinical Effects

Fatal outcome very unlikely

It is unlikely that most species in the genus Suta are able to cause significant bites in humans and there are almost no bites reported, the exception being Suta suta. There are also no studies on the venom of these snakes. For most species their small size and infrequency of encounters with humans renders them of no medical consequence. However, should bites occur, even if trivial, they should be reported.

For Suta suta, the very limited case records suggest bites cause only local pain and swelling, not systemic symptoms. There are no cases so far to prove that coagulopathy and myolysis cannot occur, so these should always be looked for. In the unlikely event that major envenoming occurred, it is unclear which antivenom would be appropriate, but a combination of CSL Tiger Snake and Polyvalent Snake Antivenoms would seem prudent.

### Special Risk Groups
#### Children

Risk to children from local or systemic envenoming is similar in nature to the risk for adults, but a childs smaller body mass implies that the comparative venom concentration will be higher, so more severe envenoming is likely, the increased risk being inversely proportional to the size of the child.

#### Pregnancy

Potential risk to foetus from systemic envenoming, similar to risk to mother

#### Elderly

The higher incidence of pre-existing diseases in the elderly and associated frailty place them at higher risk should envenoming occur. The nature and extent of increased risk will largely be determined by the nature and extent of pre-existing disease and by any medications used to treat such disease.

## Description

### Adult Length

0.50 m

Small in length, medium to moderately stout bodied snake with a moderately short to short length tail. Can grow to a maximum of about 0.85 metres. Head is slightly wide, depressed, without canthus rostralis and distinct from neck. Eyes are medium in size with vertically elliptical pupils. Dorsal scales are smooth. Dorsal scale count 23 ( 19 to 25 ) - 19 ( 17 to 21 ) - 13 ( 12 to 17 ).

### Coloration & Markings

Colour and pattern is variable over its widespread distribution ranging from pale bodied with distinctly dark head dorsum and distinct lateral head markings to dark bodied with head and body colour not differentiated and lateral head markings entirely invaded by dark pigment. Dorsal surface body colour is usually pale yellowish brown to rich red brown or greyish brown often paler laterally than vertebrally and occasionally there may be an indistinct vertebral stripe formed by slightly darker scales of the vertebral scale row. Interstitial skin is usually a darker blackish brown yielding a distinctive reticulated pattern. Head dorsum and neck ( about the first 4 to 8 transverse scale rows ) is dark brown, dark greyish brown or blackish brown. Head laterally has an irregularly dark brown bordered, white to pale brown streak commencing on the internasal and extending over and through the eye to the temporal region. The supralabials are mainly white, cream or pale brown. Head venter is white or cream, with or without some smudging of greyish brown or brown pigment. Ventral and subcaudal surface colour is usually uniform white or cream, but some populations have a greyish brown or brown midventral stripe. Iris colour is variable with olive brown, yellow brown, reddish brown or brown being most common with the outer rim similar but paler.

### Head Scales

The usual 9 supracephalic head shields, rostral wider than high, nasal entire, no loreal, nasal in contact with or separated from single preocular, preocular always higher than wide, no suboculars, 2 postoculars, temporals usually 2 + 2 ( lower anterior temporal ( a temporolabial ) is usually not in contact with postoculars and is wedged between the 5th and 6th supralabial but does not contact lip margin ), 6 supralabials ( 3rd and 4th in contact with eye, 6th the largest ) and 7 infralabials.

### Breeding

Mating occurs in summer and autumn. Viviparous, usually about 3 or 4 ( range of 2 to 7 ) young.

### Dentition

Front fangs located at anterior end of maxillary bone ( proteroglyphous ). About 3 to 7 maxillary teeth following the fang.

### Habits

Nocturnal ground dwelling snake. Shelters under logs and rocks, in abandoned animal burrows, deep soil cracks, deep leaf litter and grass hummocks. Mild disposition with a characteristic striking posture. If aggravated or provoked it will flatten its body, curl into a loose pile of horizontal loops ( spring-like curving of the body ), then strike out with single, rapid, snapping bites.

### Prey

Feeds mainly on lizards ( particularly skinks and geckos ), small snakes and small mammals.

Sexual Dimorphism

Females are larger than males.

### Region

Australia

### Countries

Australia

Australia ( Widespread distribution throughout the eastern half of Australia excluding the eastern and northern coastal regions. Eastern Northern Territory, Queensland excluding east coast, New South Wales west of the Great Dividing Range, NW Victoria and eastern South Australia excluding coastal regions ).

### Habitat

Diverse range of habitats from temperate and seasonally dry tropical woodlands, through eucalypt and acacia scrublands and arid tussock and hummock grasslands. Occupies about half to two-thirds of eastern mainland Australia ( except most coastal areas ).

## First Aid

Keep victim still, apply pressure immobilisation bandage & splint, gently wash bite area, transport to medical care

First aid for bites by Elapid snakes which do not cause significant injury at the bite site (see Comments for partial listing), but which may have the potential to cause significant general (systemic) effects, such as paralysis, muscle damage, or bleeding.

1. After ensuring the patient and onlookers have moved out of range of further strikes by the snake, the bitten person should be reassured and persuaded to lie down and remain still. Many will be terrified, fearing sudden death and, in this mood, they may behave irrationally or even hysterically. The basis for reassurance is the fact that many venomous bites do not result in envenoming, the relatively slow progression to severe envenoming (hours following elapid bites, days following viper bites) and the effectiveness of modern medical treatment.
1. The bite wound should not be tampered with in any way. Wiping it once with a damp cloth to remove surface venom is unlikely to do much harm (or good) but the wound must not be massaged. For Australian snakes only, do not wash or clean the wound in any way, as this may interfere with later venom detection once in a hospital.
1. All rings or other jewellery on the bitten limb, especially on fingers, should be removed, as they may act as tourniquets if oedema develops.
1. If the bite is on a limb, a broad bandage (even torn strips of clothing or pantyhose) should be applied over the bitten area at moderate pressure (as for a sprain; not so tight circulation is impaired), then extended to cover as much of the bitten limb as possible, including fingers or toes, going over the top of clothing rather than risking excessive limb movement by removing clothing. The bitten limb should then be immobilised as effectively as possible using an extemporised splint or sling.
1. If there is any impairment of vital functions, such as problems with respiration, airway, circulation, heart function, these must be supported as a priority. In particular, for bites causing flaccid paralysis, including respiratory paralysis, both airway and respiration may be impaired, requiring urgent and prolonged treatment, which may include the mouth to mask (mouth to mouth) technique of expired air transfer. Seek urgent medical attention.
1. Do not use Tourniquets, cut, suck or scarify the wound or apply chemicals or electric shock.
1. Avoid peroral intake, absolutely no alcohol. No sedatives outside hospital. If there will be considerable delay before reaching medical aid, measured in several hours to days, then give clear fluids by mouth to prevent dehydration.
1. If the offending snake has been killed it should be brought with the patient for identification (only relevant in areas where there are more than one naturally occurring venomous snake species), but be careful to avoid touching the head, as even a dead snake can envenom. No attempt should be made to pursue the snake into the undergrowth as this will risk further bites.
1. The snakebite victim should be transported as quickly and as passively as possible to the nearest place where they can be seen by a medically-trained person (health station, dispensary, clinic or hospital). The bitten limb must not be exercised as muscular contraction will promote systemic absorption of venom. If no motor vehicle or boat is available, the patient can be carried on a stretcher or hurdle, on the pillion or crossbar of a bicycle or on someone's back.
1. Most traditional, and many of the more recently fashionable, first aid measures are useless and potentially dangerous. These include local cauterization, incision, excision, amputation, suction by mouth, vacuum pump or syringe, combined incision and suction ("venom-ex" apparatus), injection or instillation of compounds such as potassium permanganate, phenol (carbolic soap) and trypsin, application of electric shocks or ice (cryotherapy), use of traditional herbal, folk and other remedies including the ingestion of emetic plant products and parts of the snake, multiple incisions, tattooing and so on.

## Medical Treatment

As bites cause only local effects, not including necrosis, symptomatic treatment is usually appropriate. Secondary infection is a potential risk.

As bites cause only local effects, not including necrosis, symptomatic treatment is usually appropriate. Secondary infection is a potential risk. Suta suta bites may be more severe, both locally and systemically, but do not require antivenom treatment. Admission is usually not required, but it may be advisable to observe for 12 hrs post bite, and assess for coagulopathy, myolysis, renal damage and observe for developing paralysis. While none of these major venom effects have so far been documented following Suta bites, the low number of bites studied might miss such effects if they are an uncommon sequelae.

#### Immediate Effects Management

Symptomatic care only

#### Approach to Management

While most cases will be minor, not requiring admission, some cases will be more severe, requiring admission and treatment, so assess carefully before early discharge.

#### Follow Up

#### Local Effects Management
